description:
Team Rochette is named after the rock in Jezero Crater where the Perseverance rover collected its first core samples. We are a team of two, a mother and son: a full-stack developer and a young NASA fan who is our first mission tester.

We are working on the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge with Mars to Go, a mobile-first game where kids run a Mars base on real Martian terrain and learn that math, logic and real NASA data are how you bring a crew home.
summary:
Mars to Go is a free browser game where kids ages 7–12 run a crewed base in Jezero Crater, Mars, for seven sols. Every sol they get a fixed budget of power cells to split between air, food, a radiation shield, a rover and an antenna to Earth. There is never enough for everything, so every choice shows its cost: a cell in the shield tonight is air missing tomorrow, and food planted today only arrives two sols later.

The solar storms are real. Each event is a NASA DONKI record from May 2024, and Mission 2 replays that week up to the storm Curiosity measured on Mars on May 20, 2024. Radiation counts against a dose limit, a fast storm opens a short crisis, and after each night the game explains the math and shows a real NASA fact. Every number shows its source and date.

This closes the gap the challenge describes: kids usually see a mission's outcome, never the trade-offs behind it. Here they make those trade-offs themselves, in English or Portuguese, on a phone or a computer, with no account. We tested it with an 8-year-old, and how he played changed the game.
details:
▶ PLAY NOW: https://rafaelafeijo.github.io/mars-to-go/

Free, no download, no account. Best on a computer browser; fully playable on phones and tablets too. English by default, Portuguese one tap away.

Code and documentation: https://github.com/Rafaelafeijo/mars-to-go

WHAT IT DOES

Mars to Go puts kids ages 7–12 in charge of a crewed base in Jezero Crater, Mars, for 7 sols (a sol is a Mars day). Four astronauts breathe and eat every night, and the rocket home leaves after sol 7. Every sol the child walks around the base and places power cells in five machines:

- Air machine: makes air tonight (it turns Mars CO2 into oxygen, like NASA's MOXIE).

- Greenhouse: makes food, but only two sols later (plants take time to grow).

- Shield: blocks radiation tonight, if a solar storm reaches Mars.

- Rover: drives to a real Jezero site and brings back a rock sample, but uses air and adds radiation.

- Antenna: asks Earth whether tomorrow's storm will really reach Mars; the answer arrives tonight.

There are never enough cells for everything. That is the lesson: survival in deep space is a budget.

HOW WE BUILT THE CELL LOGIC

We designed the rules on paper first (docs/en/SIM_MODEL.md), checked that no plan wins every time, and only then built screens. The rules are a small, pure TypeScript engine written test-first.

- Budget: 10 cells per sol. 3 always keep the base warm (Mars averages −59 °C, NASA Mars Fact Sheet), so 7 are free. Cells cannot be saved for later: an unused cell is lost, like solar power with no battery.

- Air: start with 10 units; the crew uses 5 per night; each Air machine cell makes 1. So keeping air level already costs 5 of the 7 free cells.

- Food: start with 6; the crew eats 2 per night; each Greenhouse cell makes 2 food, delivered two sols later. Cells planted on sols 6–7 never pay off inside the mission.

- Radiation: each real solar event has a risk from 0 to 3, taken from its DONKI class (M-class flare = 1; X-class flare or a CME that NASA's WSA-ENLIL model sends to Mars = 2; a particle storm measured at Mars = 3). Each Shield cell blocks 1 point, but only if the event really reaches Mars; the cells are spent either way.

- Dose: points that get through add to the crew's dose. Above the limit (2 points), the mission doctor sends everyone home early. Radiation also damages electronics: each point that gets through costs 1 cell on the next sol (up to 2).

- Rover: 2 cells and 2 air, plus 1 dose point, for a nearby rock (Rochette or Kodiak, real Perseverance sites). The delta front, 2.3 km away and NASA's best place to look for signs of ancient life, costs 3 air and 2 dose points.

- Antenna: 1 cell today for the answer about tomorrow. Information costs power, and it arrives late (the real radio delay is 4 to 24 minutes each way).

- As the child places cells, bars project air and food to the rocket "if every sol were like today", so a bad plan is visible before the night, not after.

- Every number lives in one file (packages/sim/src/science.ts), each with its value, unit, label (measured, scenario or simplification), source, place and date. Game rules are labeled as rules, never as measurements.

HOW WE BUILT THE MISSIONS

- Mission 1 "First sols" (guided): machines unlock over three sols (Air machine and Greenhouse, then Shield, then Rover and Antenna), with two real events from May 10–11, 2024. Goal: everyone home, one rock sample, dose within the limit.

- Mission 2 "The May storm": all machines open, and every sol is a real NASA DONKI record from the week of May 13–20, 2024, in a fixed order: an X8.7 flare, fast CMEs that NASA's model sent toward Mars, and two CMEs the model sent to the Psyche spacecraft instead (false alarms, which make asking Earth worth a cell). It ends with the May 20, 2024 storm that Curiosity's RAD measured on the surface of Mars. This time the sample must come from the delta front.

- A fast CME (1,000 km/s or more, with a Mars arrival in NASA's model) opens a crisis: the child moves cells from the Air machine, Greenhouse or Antenna into the Shield, each one showing its cost, and can call the rover back. Cadet level gives 30 seconds, Commander 10.

- Three results, each explained with that night's numbers: Mission accomplished, Mission with failures, or Early return (with the sol where things went wrong).

WHAT MAKES IT DIFFERENT

- No free choice: every option shows its cost before it is chosen.

- Real data, with a trail: every data point on screen opens a card with its NASA source and record ID, where and when it was measured, how the game uses it and what was simplified, in kid language with an everyday example. Data not measured on Mars (from the ISS, the Moon or Earth) is shown as a declared parallel, with what is different on Mars.

- Live and honest: the home screen's "The Sun this week" reads NASA DONKI live through our own small API (cached 30 minutes). If it cannot be reached, it shows a dated copy saved twice a day, and says so. Archived data is never shown as live.

- A game, not a quiz: kids learn by deciding and seeing the consequence, then reading why.

PLAYING ON A PHONE

The game runs in phone and tablet browsers: tap the ground to walk or use the on-screen direction pad, pinch to zoom, and every machine has a large action button next to it. Everything can also be done from the bottom bar, the keyboard or a screen reader. It was tested on an iPhone 16 (Safari) and a computer (Chrome); the direction pad was added after our own phone test showed that walking toward the camera was hard with taps alone.

TESTED WITH A REAL CHILD

An 8-year-old played on November 14 (mission 1) and 15 (mission 2). He skipped long text, so the screens became short bullets; he played by walking up to machines, so each machine got an action button; he thought the air machine was the crew's house, so the base got a real habitat; he asked how astronauts breathe in a suit, and that became a real NASA fact in the game. Every observation, change and commit is in docs/en/PLAYTEST.md (no name, image or voice of the child).

ACCESSIBILITY

Atkinson Hyperlegible Next font; touch targets of at least 44 px; nothing told by color alone; reduced motion respected; a gentler Cadet level for every timer. A full WCAG 2.2 AA audit is still to be done.

PRIVACY AND SAFETY

No accounts, no analytics, no personal data; progress is saved on the device. A Content Security Policy blocks any third-party request, and an automated test fails if one appears.

HOW WE KNOW IT WORKS

72 automated tests (58 for the simulation rules, including the three worked games of the design document), plus a robot that plays both missions end to end in the browser on every push. 54 documented science constants, 35 architecture decision records, and a full commit history of the weekend.

BENEFITS

Kids learn, by deciding, that survival in deep space is a budget of power, air, food and radiation under real solar weather, and that real data, with its source and date, is how astronauts and engineers decide.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React, Vite, three.js (@react-three/fiber), i18next, Hono, pnpm, Vitest, Playwright, Python (image and data preparation), GitHub Actions and Pages, Railway.

LIMITATIONS

The rules are simplifications: a power cell is not a real energy unit, risk and dose points are not real doses, and a CME arrives the same night in the game while real ones take days. The 3D terrain is an illustration inspired by Jezero, not a map. A third mission and a laboratory mode are not built yet.
